sheaf.uniqueness-weighted-module.formal: $\shW$ is the unique rain-bounded extension satisfying (T2$\partial$) and (T3$\partial$).
sheaf.uniqueness-weighted-module.technical:
Among the extensions of the Schwarzschild cometric module over the blown-up boundary, $\shW$ is the only one that is rain-bounded and satisfies the boundary versions of corank one and first-order degeneration. Rain-boundedness gives $\mathcal{M} \subseteq \shW$; if $A$ is the transition matrix from an $\mathcal{M}$-frame to the $\shW$-frame, then $\det G_{\mathcal{M}} = (\det A)^2 \det G_{\shW} = -(\det A)^2 r$.

If $A$ failed to be invertible at a boundary point, $\det G_{\mathcal{M}}$ would be $o(r)$ there, and since exactly one eigenvalue dies, the dying eigenvalue would be $o(r)$, contradicting first-order degeneration. So $A$ is invertible along the boundary and $\mathcal{M} = \shW$.
sheaf.uniqueness-weighted-module.lay: There are several ways to extend the description of the black hole's geometry up to the singularity. This result shows that only one of them stays finite for a freely falling observer and degenerates in the simplest possible way. That extension is the weighted module used throughout.
sheaf.uniqueness-weighted-module.typing_note: Kept the Schwarzschild boundary-tameness edge, which supplies the determinant of the weighted Gram.

proofs.main:
Let $\mathcal{M}$ be such an extension; rain-boundedness is exactly $\mathcal{M} \subseteq \shW$. By local freeness there is a transition matrix $A$ over $C^\infty(\Mt_u)$ expressing an $\mathcal{M}$-frame in the $\shW$-frame, invertible in the interior, and
\[
\det G_{\mathcal{M}} \;=\; (\det A)^2 \,\det G_{\shW} \;=\; -(\det A)^2\, r ,
\]
by Theorem \claimref{sheaf.schwarzschild-degeneration-boundary-tame}(1). Fix a boundary point $x_0$. If $A(x_0, 0)$ is invertible then $A$ is invertible near $x_0$ and $\mathcal{M} = \shW$ there. If not, $\det A(x_0, u) \to 0$ as $u \to 0$, so $\det G_{\mathcal{M}}(x_0, u) = o(r)$. But by (T2$\partial$) exactly one eigenvalue of $G_{\mathcal{M}}$ vanishes at $x_0$ while the others are bounded away from zero, so the dying eigenvalue is $\det G_{\mathcal{M}}$ divided by a unit: it is $o(r)$, contradicting (T3$\partial$). Hence $A$ is invertible along all of $E$, and $\mathcal{M} = \shW$.

sheaf.variable-weight-boundary-tameness-.formal:
For strict diagonal data, let $\shW$ be the $\mathcal{A}$-module with frame $\vartheta_0 = d\tau$, $\vartheta_1 = \sigma^1$, $\vartheta_2 = \tau^{p_2(x)}\sigma^2$, $\vartheta_3 = \tau^{p_3(x)}\sigma^3$ (the letter avoiding the coupling constant $\nu$). Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\shW$ is free of rank four over $\mathcal{A}$, with Gram $\operatorname{diag}(1, -\varrho c_1, -c_2, -c_3)$, $\varrho := \tau^{-2p_1(x)} \in \mathcal{A}$, extending to $E$ with corank exactly one; the radical is the line of the negative-exponent covector $\sigma^1$, and the dying entry is $-\varrho c_1$: exactly first order in the canonical defining element $\varrho$.
\item The one-sided completion applies verbatim: coupling to the dying direction with $\mu\nu < 0$ yields signature $(2,4)$ on a collar, boundary included, with the ladder pair supported exactly on $E$ and no shadow wall ($s = -1/(\varrho c_1) < 0$ throughout, so $F \geq 1$ wherever the bump is supported); the global coupling $\mu\nu = -\tfrac12$ has $\det h = c_2c_3(1 + \varrho c_1)$, nonvanishing everywhere on the collar.
\item The weights are forced pointwise: within diagonal rescalings $\tau^{a_i(x)}$, the corank-one regime \emph{with the negative-exponent axis dying at first order in $\varrho$} forces $(a_0,\dots,a_3) = (0,0,p_2,p_3)$, and the nondegenerate regime forces $(0,p_1,p_2,p_3)$: the local exponents, at each point separately. (As at Schwarzschild, naming the dying axis is read off the geometry, the negative-exponent covector being the radical of the actual degeneration; without naming it other slot assignments exist.) The exceptional Gram is $\operatorname{diag}(1,-c_1,-c_2,-c_3)|_{\tau=0}$, a smooth bundle of nondegenerate $(1,3)$ forms over $E$: the Clifford algebras of the local Kasner forms.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently the degeneration sheaf, the square-zero ideal with quotient $\Cl(1,2)$, the localised ladder pair, and the exceptional algebra all exist with position-dependent exponents, by the $C^\infty$-linearity of their constructions applied fibrewise.
sheaf.variable-weight-boundary-tameness-.technical:
For strict diagonal data with position-dependent exponents, let $\shW$ be the $\mathcal{A}$-module with frame $d\tau$, $\sigma^1$, $\tau^{p_2(x)}\sigma^2$, $\tau^{p_3(x)}\sigma^3$. It is free of rank four with Gram $\operatorname{diag}(1, -\varrho c_1, -c_2, -c_3)$, where $\varrho = \tau^{-2p_1(x)} \in \mathcal{A}$, extending to the boundary $E$ with corank exactly one, radical the negative-exponent covector $\sigma^1$, and dying entry exactly first order in $\varrho$. The one-sided completion with $\mu\nu < 0$ gives signature $(2,4)$ on a collar, boundary included, with no shadow wall; for $\mu\nu = -\tfrac12$, $\det h = c_2c_3(1 + \varrho c_1)$ never vanishes on the collar.

Within diagonal rescalings $\tau^{a_i(x)}$, the corank-one regime with the negative-exponent axis dying at first order forces $(a_0,\dots,a_3) = (0,0,p_2,p_3)$, and the nondegenerate regime forces $(0,p_1,p_2,p_3)$, at each point separately. The exceptional Gram $\operatorname{diag}(1,-c_1,-c_2,-c_3)$ at $\tau = 0$ is a smooth bundle of nondegenerate $(1,3)$ forms, so the degeneration sheaf, its square-zero ideal with quotient $\Cl(1,2)$, the ladder pair and the exceptional algebra all exist with position-dependent exponents.
sheaf.variable-weight-boundary-tameness-.lay: Near a singularity of the strictly diagonal (Kasner-like) kind, space contracts at different rates along fixed perpendicular directions, and the rates can vary from place to place. This result shows that the repair machinery developed for the black hole still works in that setting. Once the direction that degenerates is read off the geometry, the rescaling needed at each point is not a free choice: it is forced, and it equals the local contraction rates.
sheaf.variable-weight-boundary-tameness-.typing_note: Added function-linearity of the tame constructions, the C-infinity-linearity the closing consequence relies on although the source names it without a reference; both existing edges are real premises. Levels pass: the lay level no longer widens the scope to a generic singularity (the formal is for strict diagonal data), and keeps the condition that the dying axis is named from the geometry.

proofs.main: (1) Freeness: a relation $\sum c_i\vartheta_i = 0$ has interior coefficients $c_0, c_1, c_2\tau^{p_2}, c_3\tau^{p_3}$ against the coframe, all forced to vanish where $\tau > 0$, hence identically. The Gram entries: $\vartheta_2$ carries $\tau^{2p_2}(-\tau^{-2p_2}c_2) = -c_2$, likewise $\vartheta_3$; and $\varrho \in \mathcal{A}$ since $-2p_1 > 0$ pointwise. Corank and radical are read off the boundary values $\operatorname{diag}(1, 0, -c_2, -c_3)$. (2) The coupling construction is a pointwise modification of the Gram by elements of $\mathcal{A}$ and constants; the determinant identity of Lemma \claimref{sheaf.determinant-identity-blow-up-expansion} is algebraic, valid over any commutative ring, with $s = G^{-1}(e,e) = -1/(\varrho c_1)$ here; the boundary signature is Lemma \claimref{sheaf.wall-gram} with $\mu\nu < 0$; the global determinant is the same identity at $\beta \equiv 1$. (3) The diagonal entries have $\tau$-orders $(0, -2p_1, -2p_2, -2p_3)$; each regime's named profile prescribes the target order of every slot, and the resulting equations are linear with the displayed unique solutions. All computational clauses are verified as exact rational-function identities at three rational Kasner points, with the ladder pair on all $64$ boundary states (the section “Machine verification”). The closing consequence is \claimref{sheaf.function-linearity-tame-constructions}: each construction is $C^\infty$-linear over the base and so applies fibrewise to data with position-dependent exponents.

sheaf.wall-class.formal: There is a natural invariant of tame walls, built from $w(\Sig)$ and the torsion of the pair $(\shL, N^*\Sig)$, with the properties: (a) it vanishes iff some completion standard outside a collar is nondegenerate on \emph{both} sides (by Theorem \claimref{sheaf.conservation-degeneracy-absolute-form}, it must therefore be nonvanishing whenever both sides are nonempty and the clock positions differ); (b) it is conserved under the wall induction of Lemma \claimref{sheaf.tame-wall-induction}, each iteration transferring it to the next shadow wall while shifting both clock coordinates by the rung; (c) it refines, at sheaf level, the conservation-of-obstruction conjecture of \cite[Conj.~7.9]{ButlerT1}, whose fibre-level content is the mod-8 obstruction of the transport rules. Theorem \claimref{sheaf.conservation-degeneracy-absolute-form} proves the existence half of (a) in signature terms; the conjecture is that the signature mismatch is the coarse part of a finer, torsion-sensitive class whose vanishing is also sufficient.
sheaf.wall-class.technical:
Conjecture: tame walls carry a natural invariant, built from $w(\Sig)$ and the torsion of the pair $(\shL, N^*\Sig)$, which (a) vanishes exactly when some completion standard outside a collar is nondegenerate on both sides, and so is nonzero whenever both sides are nonempty and the clock positions differ; (b) is conserved under the wall induction, passing to each shadow wall with both clock coordinates shifted by the rung; and (c) refines at sheaf level the conservation-of-obstruction conjecture, whose fibre-level content is the mod-8 obstruction of the transport rules.

The absolute form of conservation of degeneracy already proves one half of (a) in signature terms. The conjecture is that this signature mismatch is the coarse part of a finer, torsion-sensitive class whose vanishing is also sufficient.
sheaf.wall-class.lay: At a mild (tame) wall whose two sides are both present and carry different clock positions, every repair leaves degeneracy somewhere, and a mismatch of signatures explains why. This conjecture proposes a finer invariant of the wall, sensitive to subtle topological twisting, that would detect exactly when a repair can succeed on both sides. It would be carried unchanged from each wall to the next shadow wall.
sheaf.wall-class.typing_note: Conjecture with lineage already set from its three context references; no edges or status change. Levels pass: the lay level no longer says every repair of any degenerate wall fails; it now keeps the tame-wall setting and the conditions (both sides nonempty, clock positions differ) under which the proved signature half applies.

sheaf.weights-are-forced-are-kasner-expo.technical:
Rescale the Schwarzschild coordinate coframe diagonally by powers $r^{a_i}$ and ask that the derived cometric of the Schwarzschild gravitational field on flat spacetime, read on the rescaled coframe, extend continuously to the singular boundary $E$. The diagonal cometric entries have $r$-orders $(-1, +1, -2)$, which the rescaling shifts to $(2a_r - 1,\, 2a_t + 1,\, 2a_\theta - 2)$, so prescribing the target order of each slot fixes every weight by a linear solve. A corank-one limit in which the Killing-time entry dies at first order forces $(a_r, a_t, a_\theta) = (\tfrac12, 0, 1)$, the degeneration-sheaf regime; a nondegenerate limit forces $(\tfrac12, -\tfrac12, 1)$, the exceptional regime.

Which entry dies is read off the gravitational field, since the radical of the actual degeneration is the Killing-time covector; without naming it other assignments exist, so uniqueness is per named profile. Converted to proper time $\tau_{\mathrm{p}} \propto r^{3/2}$, the exceptional weights become the Kasner exponents $(-\tfrac13, \tfrac23, \tfrac23)$, with $\sum p_i = \sum p_i^2 = 1$. Within the diagonal class, the weights of the anisotropic completion are therefore forced, not chosen.
sheaf.weights-are-forced-are-kasner-expo.lay: Near the centre of a Schwarzschild black hole the gravitational field stretches lengths in some directions and squeezes them in others. To describe it smoothly up to the singularity one can rescale each coordinate direction by a power of the radius, and this result shows that, among such direction-by-direction rescalings, the powers are not a free choice: once the limiting behaviour the field dictates is imposed, only one set works. Measured in the infalling observer's own time, those powers are exactly the Kasner exponents that describe how space distorts near such a singularity.
sheaf.weights-are-forced-are-kasner-expo.typing_note: Added the three cited results because the regime profiles, the named dying Killing-time direction and the Kasner identification are taken from them; no standard route, since only the Kasner exponents are classical and they enter as an imported premise, not as a standard derivation of the forcing. Levels pass: conditions already kept.

proofs.main: The cometric entries are those of the derived cometric of the Schwarzschild gravitational field, read through Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}(i). The diagonal cometric entries have $r$-orders $(-1, +1, -2)$; a rescaling shifts these to $(2a_r - 1,\, 2a_t + 1,\, 2a_\theta - 2)$, and each regime's stated profile prescribes the target order of every slot ($(0, 1, 0)$ for the degeneration regime of \claimref{sheaf.schwarzschild-degeneration-boundary-tame} with the Killing-time slot dying, $(0,0,0)$ for the exceptional regime of \claimref{sheaf.exceptional-algebra-black-hole}), determining each weight by the invertible linear relation displayed. The script confirms the two solutions by exhaustive search of the stated profiles over the grid $\tfrac16\mathbb{Z} \cap [-2,2]$ (a finite check of the linear solve, not a substitute for it) and verifies the conversion and the Kasner sum rules of \claimref{sheaf.kasner-data-interior} exactly.

At a point of $E$ with the collar constants $\mu, 
u$ and the bump held fixed, call a vector $u'$ with $k(u') = 1$ a \emph{candidate value} for the dying direction $k$; the candidates form an affine space over $\ker k$. For every $\lambda \in \ker k$ the composite $	heta_\lambda := \hat g_\lambda \circ \Phi_\lambda^{-1}$, with $\hat g_\lambda := g_\lambda \oplus \id$ on $T = \shW \oplus \operatorname{span}\{
O, 
Inf\}$, is an automorphism of the completed structure $(T, h_u, k)$: an $h_u$-isometry restricting to $g_\lambda$ on $\shW$ and fixing $k$, hence an automorphism of the completed Clifford algebra preserving its grading and its degeneration subalgebra. Its contragredient action on vectors, $(	heta_\lambda|_{\shW})^{-\mathsf{T}} = \id - \lambda \otimes k$, translates every candidate by $-\lambda$. A natural assignment of a candidate value, one per completed structure and commuting with automorphisms, would therefore be a fixed point of a free translation action of $(\ker k, +)$: none exists. Nor is a ladder partner for $k$ any more canonical than a value: for $\lambda 
eq 0$, $h_u(k, x) = 0$ for every $x \in \operatorname{Fix}(	heta_\lambda)$, whereas a ladder partner has $h_u(k, x) = 	frac12$; and the construction attaches to each candidate $u' = u + v$ the partner $\Phi_v(k^*) = k^* + 	frac12	ilde v$ of the transversal-independence theorem, injectively in $v$. Inf)$ and the partner $k^* = 
O/2
u$ are choices inside it, not part of it. O) = 
O + 
u	ilde v$, $\Phi_v(
Inf) = 
Inf + \mu	ilde v$, an isometry $(T, h_{u+v}) 	o (T, h_u)$ satisfying the cocycle $\Phi^u_v \circ \Phi^{u+v}_w = \Phi^u_{v+w}$, so that the completions built on all transversals are canonically identified, at the wall, by a coherent system of isomorphisms preserving the form, the grading and the degeneration subalgebra but neither the frame nor the ladder pair. singularity.imported-no-equivariant-valu.technical:
At a point of the wall $E$, with the collar constants $\mu, \nu$ and the bump fixed, a candidate value for the dying direction $k$ is a vector $u'$ with $k(u') = 1$, and the candidates form an affine space over $\ker k$. For each $\lambda \in \ker k$ the composite $\theta_\lambda = \hat g_\lambda \circ \Phi_\lambda^{-1}$ of the base unipotent $g_\lambda(\alpha) = \alpha + \alpha(\lambda)k$ with the inverse of the transversal intertwiner is an automorphism of the completed structure $(T, h_u, k)$ that fixes $k$ and preserves the grading and the degeneration subalgebra. Its action on vectors is $\id - \lambda \otimes k$, which translates every candidate by $-\lambda$.

A value assignment natural under automorphisms would be a fixed point of this free translation action of $(\ker k, +)$, and none exists. A ladder partner for $k$ is no more canonical: for $\lambda \neq 0$ every fixed vector $x$ of $\theta_\lambda$ has $h_u(k, x) = 0$, whereas a partner has $h_u(k, x) = \tfrac12$. The statement is imported verbatim, up to notation, from the earlier sheaf paper, where it is machine-verified on the Schwarzschild boundary data.
singularity.imported-no-equivariant-valu.lay: At the wall where the black-hole geometry degenerates, one direction loses its partner. One might hope to supply a definite classical replacement for it, but the symmetries of the completed structure shift every candidate replacement without leaving any in place. So no replacement, and no partner, can be chosen in a way that respects those symmetries. This is carried over from earlier in the series.

synthesis.imported-line-bundles-classifi.formal: (i) \emph{(Classification.)} Every real line bundle $L$ over a paracompact space $X$ is isomorphic to $f^{*}\gamma$ for a map $f : X \to \mathbb{RP}^{\infty}$, $\gamma$ the tautological line bundle, unique up to homotopy, and $w_{1}(L) = f^{*}w_{1}(\gamma)$. (ii) \emph{(Cellular approximation.)} Every map between CW complexes is homotopic to a cellular map, one sending the $d$-skeleton into the $d$-skeleton. (iii) \emph{(Consequence.)} If $X$ is a CW complex of dimension $d$, $f$ may be taken with image in $\mathbb{RP}^{d}$, so $L \cong f^{*}\gamma_{d}$ with $\gamma_{d} \subset \mathbb{RP}^{d} \times \R^{d+1}$, and $L$ is a subbundle of the trivial bundle $X \times \R^{d+1}$. Topological statements, flagged as such. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[\S 5]{MilnorStasheff1974} (classifying spaces); \cite[Theorem 4.8]{Hatcher2002} (cellular approximation).
synthesis.imported-line-bundles-classifi.technical: Line bundles over a space are classified by maps into infinite real projective space, the space of all lines. A map from a $d$-dimensional complex can always be deformed to land in the $d$-dimensional projective space, whose lines sit in a fixed $(d+1)$-dimensional space. So every line bundle over a $d$-dimensional base sits inside a trivial bundle of rank $d+1$. The series uses this as the upper bound on the number of rungs a wall needs.
synthesis.imported-line-bundles-classifi.lay: Any twisting family of lines over a space can be fitted inside an untwisted family of slightly larger spaces, one dimension more than the space itself. This is the classical fact behind an upper limit the series puts on how much structure a degenerating wall needs.

imported_from.citation: J. W. Milnor and J. D. Stasheff, Characteristic Classes, Annals of Mathematics Studies 76, Princeton University Press (1974).
A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Cambridge University Press (2002).

synthesis.imported-stiefel-connectivity-.technical: Frames of $k$ orthonormal vectors in $m$ dimensions form a space with no holes of dimension below $m - k$, so on a small enough complex every family of such frames can be deformed to a constant one. The Grassmannian of $k$-planes classifies rank-$k$ bundles in the same range: over a complex of dimension below $m - k$, two $k$-plane subbundles of a trivial $m$-dimensional bundle can be deformed into each other exactly when they are isomorphic bundles. Both are standard results of bundle theory.
synthesis.imported-stiefel-connectivity-.lay: Two standard facts from topology: a family of frames in a space of many dimensions can always be straightened out over a small enough base, and over such a base the only thing that distinguishes two families of planes is whether they are twisted the same way. The series uses them to show that two ways of filling a wall can be deformed into one another.

synthesis.imported-whitney-product-formu.formal: (i) \emph{(Whitney product formula.)} For real vector bundles $E$, $F$ over a paracompact space, the total Stiefel-Whitney classes satisfy $w(E \oplus F) = w(E) \cup w(F)$, $w = 1 + w_{1} + w_{2} + \cdots$, and $w(\varepsilon^{k}) = 1$ for a trivial bundle. (ii) \emph{(Projective space.)} $H^{*}(\mathbb{RP}^{n}; \mathbb{Z}_{2}) = \mathbb{Z}_{2}[a]/(a^{n+1})$ with $a = w_{1}(\gamma_{n})$ the class of the tautological line bundle $\gamma_{n} \subset \mathbb{RP}^{n} \times \R^{n+1}$; in particular $a^{n} \neq 0$. (iii) \emph{(Euler sequence.)} $T\mathbb{RP}^{n} \oplus \varepsilon^{1} \cong (n+1)\,\gamma_{n}$, so $w(\mathbb{RP}^{n}) = (1 + a)^{n+1}$. Topological statements about bundles over the space, flagged as such. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[\S 4]{MilnorStasheff1974}.
synthesis.imported-whitney-product-formu.technical: Three classical facts of bundle theory. Stiefel-Whitney classes multiply when bundles are added, so a bundle that adds to a trivial one has the inverse total class. The mod-two cohomology of real projective $n$-space is generated by the class of its tautological line, whose powers survive up to the $n$-th. And the tangent bundle of projective space plus one trivial line is $n+1$ copies of the tautological line, which gives its total class. The series uses them to bound how many rungs a wall whose dying line twists needs, and to show that the bound is reached on a projective wall.
synthesis.imported-whitney-product-formu.lay: Mathematicians attach to each family of lines or planes over a space a set of invariants that detect twisting. These facts say how the invariants combine when families are put together, and compute them for the simplest twisted space, the projective space of lines through a point.

synthesis.lens-space-wall-rung-count-see.formal:
Let $(M, G)$ be a tame corank-one degeneration (\claimref{sheaf.tameness}) with $\dim M = 4$, compact wall $\Sig \cong L(4,1) = S^{3}/\mathbb{Z}_{4}$, physical side $\Mp$ of signature $(p,q)$, $p \geq 1$, dying line $\shL$ with $x := w_1(\shL) \neq 0$, and $k(\Sig)$ the least number of rungs of a completion in the sense of \claimref{synthesis.wall-rung-count-is-height-of-dying-line-class}. Then $x^{2} = 0$, so $\operatorname{ht}(x) = 2$, and:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{(Indefinite side.)} If $q \geq 1$, then $k(\Sig) = 2 = \operatorname{ht}(x)$: the lower bound of the parent claim is attained, by a completion whose wall form rotates one direction of the physical metric of sign opposite to the dying direction into the rungs.
\item \emph{(Definite side.)} If $q = 0$, then $k(\Sig) = 3 = e(\shL) > \operatorname{ht}(x)$.
\item \emph{(The deciding datum.)} The wall $T^{3}$ with $x \neq 0 = x^{2}$ pulled back from a circle has $k = 2$ with a definite physical side. So two walls with the same mod-2 data ($w(\Sig) = 1$, $x \neq 0 = x^{2}$) and the same signature need different numbers of rungs: in the definite case the rung count is not a function of $W(\Sig) = (w(\Sig), x)$ and the signature; what separates the two walls is whether $\shL \oplus \shL$ is trivial, which on $L(4,1)$ it is not.
\end{enumerate}
Classical inputs (cited from memory, not imported): $V_{k}(\R^{m})$ is $(m-k-1)$-connected, and $[X, \mathrm{Gr}_{k}(\R^{m})]$ is the set of isomorphism classes of rank-$k$ bundles over a complex $X$ of dimension less than $m - k$.
synthesis.lens-space-wall-rung-count-see.technical:
The parent claim bounds the rung count of a tame wall between the height of the dying line's class and the least rank of a trivial bundle containing the dying line, and leaves the lens space $L(4,1)$ open: there the class squares to zero, so the lower bound is two, but the doubled dying line is not trivial, so the dying line does not sit in the trivial bundle of rank two that two rungs offer. The key is the adjoint map of rotors. On unit rotors of $\Cl(3,0)$, left multiplication by the half-turn rotor $e_2e_3$, whose square is $-1$, generates the $\mathbb{Z}_4$ with quotient $L(4,1)$, and the frame $R e_a \tilde R$ transforms by $\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1)$: its first row is a global section of the trivial line and its other two rows are sections of the dying line, so $\underline{\R} \oplus \shL \oplus \shL$ is trivial with an explicit frame.

When the physical side is indefinite, the wall form takes the hyperbolic partner of the dying line and one further negative direction from the rungs, built with this frame; its negative bundle is then the negative part of the physical metric plus $\shL \oplus \shL$, which the frame identifies with the negative bundle of the standard form. A form with that negative bundle can be joined to the standard form through nondegenerate forms, by the connectivity of Stiefel manifolds, and that join is a two-rung completion. When the physical side is definite there is no direction to borrow: the necessity argument forces $\shL \oplus \shL$ trivial, which fails because an odd map from $S^3$ to the punctured plane would wind by half a turn per quarter turn of the fibre, so three rungs are needed and suffice, the dying line being the second row of the frame inside the trivial bundle of rank three. On a three-torus with the same mod-2 data the doubled dying line is trivial and two rungs suffice even with a definite side, so with a definite side the rung count separates walls the mod-2 classes do not; with an indefinite side it is the mod-2 height on both walls. All of this assumes the tame-wall setting of the parent claim.
synthesis.lens-space-wall-rung-count-see.lay: At a wall where the geometry changes signature, extra pairs of directions (rungs) can repair the degeneracy, and an earlier result bounded how many are needed by how the dying direction twists. The open test case was a wall shaped like the lens space $L(4,1)$, where the bounds were two and three. The answer depends on the side we live on. If that side has directions of both signs, as ordinary spacetime does, two rungs suffice: the repair borrows one direction of the opposite sign from the physical geometry and twists it together with the rungs, using the rotation of space by a half turn, whose spinor squares to minus one. If that side is definite there is nothing to borrow and three rungs are needed. A wall shaped like a three-torus with the same simple twist needs only two either way. So when the side we live on is indefinite, the price is set by the simple twist class alone; only when that side is definite is the price set by a finer property of the twist (whether the doubled dying direction can be untwisted, classically an integer-valued class) that the simple twist class does not record.

proofs.main:
\emph{Setting and tools.} Throughout, $(M,G)$ satisfies (T1) to (T3) of \claimref{sheaf.tameness}. We use the definitions, tools (a), (b) and the necessity and sufficiency clauses (1), (2) of \claimref{synthesis.wall-rung-count-is-height-of-dying-line-class}: a $k$-rung completion is a smooth symmetric form $h$ on $T_k = T^*M \oplus \underline{\R}^{2k}$ over $\Mp$, nondegenerate on $\Mp$ including $\Sig$, with $h|_{T^*M} = G$ along $\Sig$ and $h = G \perp H_k$ outside the collar $C \cong \Sig \times [-1,1]$; $N(\cdot)$ and $P(\cdot)$ denote maximal negative and positive subbundles. On the physical half of the collar $P(G) \cong P(\overline G) \oplus \shL$ and $N(G) \cong N(\overline G)$, with $\overline G$ the induced form on $T^*M|_\Sig/\shL$ of signature $(p-1, q)$ (\claimref{sheaf.degeneration-sheaf}; proof of \claimref{synthesis.wall-class-one-rung-obstruction}). Line bundles with equal $w_1$ are isomorphic, and $w$ is multiplicative (Fact \claimref{sheaf.imported-real-line-bundles}; \cite[\S 4]{MilnorStasheff1974}). Two classical inputs (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-stiefel-connectivity-and-grassmannian-classification}): (S) the Stiefel manifold $V_k(\R^m)$ of $k$-frames is $(m-k-1)$-connected, so a map from a complex of dimension at most $m - k - 1$ into it is null-homotopic; (G) for a complex $X$ of dimension less than $m - k$, homotopy classes of maps $X \to \mathrm{Gr}_k(\R^m)$ correspond to isomorphism classes of rank-$k$ bundles over $X$ \cite[\S 5]{MilnorStasheff1974}. We also use the elementary fact (F) that the space of nondegenerate symmetric forms of signature $(P,Q)$ on $\R^{P+Q}$ retracts onto $\mathrm{Gr}_Q(\R^{P+Q})$ by sending a form to its negative eigenspace, the fibre (forms with a given negative eigenspace) being convex, and that for a fixed form the maximal negative subspaces form a contractible set (graphs of contractions over one of them); so two continuous families of forms of the same signature over a complex are joined by a continuous family of such forms exactly when their negative subbundles are homotopic as sections of the Grassmann bundle, and a continuous join can be smoothed and made to agree with given smooth families near its ends.

\emph{The adjoint frame.} In $\Cl(3,0)$ let $B := e_2 e_3$, so $B\tilde B = 1$ and $B^{2} = -1$: $B$ is the rotor of a half turn about $e_1$, of order four in the rotor group. Left multiplication by $B$ acts freely on the unit rotors $S^{3}$ with quotient $\Sig = L(4,1)$ (identifying rotors with unit quaternions, it is $(z_1, z_2) \mapsto (iz_1, iz_2)$). For a rotor $R$ let $O(R)_{ab} := \langle e_a\, R e_b \tilde R\rangle$; by \claimref{std-algebra.spin-double-cover}, $O(R) \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ and $O(-R) = O(R)$, and $O(BR) = O(B)O(R) = D\,O(R)$ with $D = \mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1)$, since $B e_1 \tilde B = e_1$, $B e_{2,3} \tilde B = -e_{2,3}$. A function $f$ on $S^{3}$ with $f(BR) = f(R)$ is a function on $\Sig$, and one with $f(BR) = -f(R)$ is a section of the line bundle $\shL_B$ whose holonomy around the generator of $\pi_1(\Sig) = \mathbb{Z}_4$ is $-1$; $w_1(\shL_B)$ is the nonzero element of $H^{1}(\Sig;\mathbb{Z}_2) = \mathbb{Z}_2$, so $\shL \cong \shL_B$. Hence: the rows $O_1, O_2, O_3$ of $O$ are a global orthonormal frame of the trivial $\underline{\R}^{3}$, with $O_1$ a section of the trivial line and $O_2, O_3$ sections of $\shL$; that is,
\[
\underline{\R} \oplus \shL \oplus \shL \cong \underline{\R}^{3} \quad\text{explicitly, and}\quad \shL \cong \operatorname{span}(O_2) \subset \underline{\R}^{3}. \tag{$*$}
\]
Taking Stiefel-Whitney classes in $(*)$, $(1+x)^{2} = 1$, so $x^{2} = 0$ and $\operatorname{ht}(x) = 2$. Tensoring $(*)$ with $\shL$ (and $\shL \otimes \shL \cong \underline\R$) gives $\shL \oplus \underline{\R}^{2} \cong \shL^{\oplus 3}$. The left-invariant coframe $\sigma_a$ of $S^{3}$ is invariant under left multiplication, so it descends: $T^*\Sig$ is trivial, and since tame walls are two-sided, $T^*M|_\Sig$ and $T_k|_\Sig$ are trivial bundles.

\emph{$\shL \oplus \shL$ is not trivial.} A trivialisation would give a nowhere-zero section, i.e.\ a continuous $f : S^{3} \to \mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ with $f(BR) = -f(R)$. Since $S^{3}$ is simply connected, $f = |f| e^{i\varphi}$ with $\varphi$ continuous and real; then $\varphi(BR) - \varphi(R) \in \pi + 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ is a continuous function on a connected space, hence a constant $(2j+1)\pi$, and applying it four times, $0 = \varphi(B^{4}R) - \varphi(R) = 4(2j+1)\pi$, a contradiction.

\emph{(2), the definite side.} If $q = 0$ then $N(\overline G) = 0$ and a two-rung completion would give, by clause (1) of the parent claim, a line bundle $N$ with $\shL \oplus N \cong \underline{\R}^{2}$; then $w_1(N) = x$, so $N \cong \shL$ and $\shL \oplus \shL$ is trivial, which is false. With one rung even less is possible ($x \neq 0$). So $k(\Sig) \geq 3$; and by $(*)$, $\shL$ lies in the trivial bundle of rank three, so clause (2) of the parent claim (the coupling of \claimref{sheaf.one-sided-completion} with twisted collar data, its twist confined to the collar) gives a three-rung completion: $k(\Sig) = 3 = e(\shL)$ ($e(\shL) \geq 3$ by the same argument). Such walls exist: on $M = \Sig \times \R$ with $\ell := O_2 \cdot \sigma$ and the cometric $G_t = A - (1 - t) A(\pi\,\cdot, \pi\,\cdot)$ of the projective-wall construction of the parent claim ($A$ the Euclidean metric in the frame $(\sigma_a, dt)$, $\pi$ the projection on $\ell$), the wall $t = 0$ is tame with dying line $\operatorname{span}(\ell) \cong \shL$, positive definite side $t > 0$. The check builds the three-rung form of clause (2) with $\shL$ embedded as $O_2$ in the null space of $H_3$ and verifies at exact rotors and several $t, \beta$: single valuedness under $R \mapsto BR$, $h|_{T^*M} = G$, $\det h = 2\mu\nu\beta^{2} - t$ and signature $(7,3)$ for $t \geq 0$.

\emph{(1), the indefinite side.} Let $q \geq 1$. Over $\Sig$ choose a complement $V_1$ of $\shL$ in $T^*M|_\Sig$, so $G|_{V_1} = \overline G$, and write the rung summand $\underline{\R}^{4}$ with basis $r_1, \dots, r_4$ (any fixed basis, for instance $a_1, a_2, b_1, b_2$ of $H \perp H$). Over $S^{3}$ put $g_a := \sum_b O_{ab}\, r_{b+1}$ ($a = 1,2,3$): $g_1$ descends to $\Sig$, while $g_2, g_3$ are sections of $\shL \otimes \underline{\R}^{4}$, i.e.\ odd. Let $\theta$ be a local generator of $\shL$; $W := \shL \oplus \underline{\R}^{4}$ has the local frame $(\theta, r_1, g_1, g_2, g_3)$. Define $h_W$ on $W$ by
\[
h_W(\theta,\theta) = 0,\quad h_W(\theta, g_2) = 1,\quad h_W(g_2,g_2) = 0,\quad h_W(g_3,g_3) = -1,\quad h_W(r_1,r_1) = h_W(g_1,g_1) = 1,
\]
all other pairings of frame vectors zero. Under $\theta \mapsto -\theta$ together with $R \mapsto BR$ (which sends $g_2, g_3$ to $-g_2, -g_3$) every entry is unchanged, so $h_W$ is a well-defined form on $W$ over $\Sig$, of signature $(3,2)$: the hyperbolic pair $(\theta, g_2)$ plus $(+,+,-)$. Set $h_0 := \overline G|_{V_1} \perp h_W$ on $T_2|_\Sig = V_1 \oplus W$. Then $h_0|_{T^*M} = \overline G \oplus 0 = G$ along $\Sig$, since $\theta$ spans the radical of $G$ there; $h_0$ is nondegenerate of signature $(p-1,q) + (3,2) = (p+2, q+2)$, the signature of $G \perp H_2$ on the physical side; and
\[
N(h_0) = N(\overline G) \oplus \operatorname{span}(\theta - g_2) \oplus \operatorname{span}(g_3) \cong N(\overline G) \oplus \shL \oplus \shL, \qquad P(h_0) = P(\overline G) \oplus \operatorname{span}(\theta + \tfrac12 g_2) \oplus \operatorname{span}(r_1, g_1) \cong P(\overline G) \oplus \shL \oplus \underline{\R}^{2}.
\]
On the other side, at $\Sig \times \{1\}$ the standard form $h_1 := G \perp H_2$ has $N(h_1) \cong N(\overline G) \oplus \underline{\R}^{2}$ and $P(h_1) \cong P(\overline G) \oplus \shL \oplus \underline{\R}^{2}$, transported to $\Sig$ by tool (b). Here $m := \operatorname{rank} T_2 = 8$ and $\dim \Sig = 3$.

Case $q \geq 2$. Then $P(h_0) \cong P(h_1)$, of rank $p + 2$, and $m - (p+2) = q + 2 \geq 4 > 3$, so by (G) the positive subbundles of $h_0$ and $h_1$ are homotopic as maps $\Sig \to \mathrm{Gr}_{p+2}(\R^{8})$ (in the trivialisation of $T_2|_\Sig$), and by (F), applied to $-h$, $h_0$ and $h_1$ are joined by a family of nondegenerate forms over $\Sig \times [0,1]$.

Case $q = 1$, so $p = 3$ and $N(\overline G)$ is a line bundle, trivial or $\shL$ (these are the only two, as $H^{1}(\Sig;\mathbb{Z}_2) = \mathbb{Z}_2$). If it is trivial, $N(h_0) \cong \underline\R \oplus \shL \oplus \shL \cong \underline{\R}^{3} \cong N(h_1)$ by $(*)$; if it is $\shL$, $N(h_0) \cong \shL^{\oplus 3} \cong \shL \oplus \underline{\R}^{2} \cong N(h_1)$ by $(*)$ tensored with $\shL$. Now $m - 3 = 5 > 3$, so (G) and (F) join $h_0$ to $h_1$ as before. (When $N(\overline G)$ is trivial the frame of $N(h_0)$ is explicit: with $n = (\nu_0, \theta - g_2, g_3)$, $\nu_0$ a unit section of $N(\overline G)$, the vectors $f_a := \sum_b O_{ba}\, n_b$ are invariant under $R \mapsto BR$, $\theta \mapsto -\theta$, so they descend, and the map $\Sig \to V_3(\R^{8})$ they define is null-homotopic by (S); this is the instance the check verifies.)

In both cases let $h(\cdot, t)$, $0 \leq t \leq \frac12$, be the join, reparametrised and smoothed so that it equals $h_0$ at $t = 0$ and agrees with $G_t \perp H_2$ near $t = \frac12$ (that family is nondegenerate for $t > 0$ and is homotopic to $h_1$ through itself), and put $h := G \perp H_2$ for $t \geq \frac12$. This is smooth on $T_2$ over $\Mp$, nondegenerate everywhere including $\Sig$, restricts to $G$ along $\Sig$ and is standard outside $C$: a two-rung completion. With the lower bound of the parent claim, $k(\Sig) = 2 = \operatorname{ht}(x)$.

The check verifies the instance $M = \Sig \times \R$, $G_t = (I - (1-t)\,\ell\ell^{T}) \perp (-dt^{2})$ in the frame $(\sigma_a, dt)$, $\ell = O_2$, which is a tame wall with physical side of signature $(3,1)$ and $N(\overline G) = \operatorname{span}(dt)$: at seven exact rational rotors (not normalised; $O$ is computed as $R e_b \tilde R/(R\tilde R)$ with $GA$), $O$ is orthogonal with $\det O = 1$, $O(BR) = DO(R)$ and $O(-R) = O(R)$; $h_0$ in the fixed basis $(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3,dt,a_1,a_2,b_1,b_2)$ satisfies $h_0(BR) = h_0(R)$, its restriction to $T^*M$ has radical $\ell$ and signature $(2,1,1)$, $h_0$ has signature $(5,3)$ like $G_1 \perp H_2$, the Gram matrix of $(dt, \theta - g_2, g_3)$ is $\mathrm{diag}(-1,-2,-1)$, and the frame $f$ is invariant with Gram of signature $(0,3)$.

\emph{(3), the comparison wall.} On $\Sig' = T^{3}$ with $x$ pulled back from the first circle, the half-angle frame $(c, s) = (\cos\frac\varphi2, \sin\frac\varphi2)$ embeds $\shL$ in $\underline{\R}^{2}$ (the stored torus wall's frame), so clause (2) of the parent claim gives a two-rung completion for the definite cometric $G_t = I - (1-t)\,\ell\ell^{T}$, $\ell = (c, s, 0, 0)$; the check verifies single valuedness under $(c,s) \mapsto (-c,-s)$, $\det h = t - 2\mu\nu$ and signature $(6,2)$ for $t \geq 0$ at rational half-angle points. Both $T^{3}$ and $L(4,1)$ are parallelizable ($w = 1$) and carry $x \neq 0 = x^{2}$, with definite physical sides; the rung counts are $2$ and $3$. So in the definite case the rung count is not a function of $(w(\Sig), x)$, its powers and the signature; by the argument of (2), with a definite side two rungs suffice exactly when $x \neq 0$ and $\shL \oplus \shL$ is trivial.

\emph{Remark (classical, from memory; not used above).} $\shL \oplus \shL$ is the realification of $\shL \otimes \mathbb{C}$, whose first Chern class is the integral Bockstein $\beta x \in H^{2}(\Sig;\mathbb{Z})$, a $2$-torsion class with $x^{2} = \beta x \bmod 2$. On $L(4,1)$, $\beta x = 2 \in \mathbb{Z}_4$; on $T^{3}$, $\beta x = 0$. So the datum that decides the definite case is the torsion class $\beta x$, which the mod-2 class $W(\Sig)$ does not record: a torsion-sensitive invariant in the sense of the wall-class conjecture \claimref{sheaf.wall-class}. Why the invariant has to be a class of the bundle of algebras and not of fibrewise module data: at a point of the wall the Clifford algebra of $G$ is that of a form with a one-dimensional radical, the ideal generated by the dying line is nilpotent (it is spanned by the blades with a factor in the radical, Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.radical-ideal-and-quotient}(i), (ii)), so it acts as zero on every simple module, and the simple modules at the wall are those of the quotient by it, the Clifford algebra of $\overline G$ (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.radical-ideal-and-quotient}(iii)); no fibrewise module datum sees $\shL$, which enters only through how the fibres are glued. In the language of clause (4) of the parent claim, the jump of the Clifford sheaf across the wall is $\Cl(\shL \otimes \R^{0,2})$, a bundle of graded algebras whose odd part is $\shL \oplus \shL$: it is trivial as a bundle of graded algebras exactly when $\shL\oplus\shL$ is, so with a definite physical side two rungs suffice exactly when the Clifford jump is trivial as a bundle (for $x \neq 0$), while (argued, on $L(4,1)$ and the torus) its graded Morita class, by Donovan and Karoubi (from memory) the clock step with $x^{2}$, is what the indefinite count sees.

synthesis.tameness-splits-regularity-and.formal:
Let $G$ be a smooth symmetric form on $T^*M$ and $\Sig$ its degeneracy locus. In a local frame $(k, m_1, \dots, m_{n-1})$ along a transversal with parameter $\tau$, $\Sig = \{\tau = 0\}$, write the Gram matrix as $\begin{psmallmatrix} \lambda & b^{\mathsf T} \\ b & G_1 \end{psmallmatrix}$ with $G_1$ invertible near $\Sig$ and $k$ spanning the radical on $\Sig$ (so $\lambda = b = 0$ there), and let $S := \lambda - b^{\mathsf T} G_1^{-1} b = \det G / \det G_1$ be the Schur complement.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{(Regularity.)} At a point of $\Sig$ of corank one, $d(\det G) = \det G_1 \cdot \delta(k \otimes k)$, with $\delta$ the transversality datum of Lemma \claimref{sheaf.invariant-form-t3}; at a point of corank at least two, $d(\det G) = 0$. Hence (T1)-(T3) of the tameness hypothesis hold along $\Sig$ if and only if, in some (equivalently every) local frame, $\det G$ vanishes exactly on $\Sig$ with nonzero differential there: tameness is the statement that the degeneracy locus is the regular zero set of $\det G$, and (T3) is the statement that $S$ vanishes to first order. (At a point of corank at least two the zero of $\det G$ is therefore never simple; the behaviour of transverse corank-two points is the subject of the result filed alongside, synthesis.transverse-corank-two-walls-are-wild.)
\item \emph{(Completion without (T3).)} Assume (T1) and (T2), $\Sig$ compact, $w_1(\shL) = 0$, and that $S > 0$ on the physical side $\Mp$, of signature $(p,q)$. Then for $s := G^{-1}(e,e)$ of the collar data, exactly,
\[
s \;=\; \frac{(1 - c)^2}{S} + B, \qquad c := b^{\mathsf T} G_1^{-1} e', \quad B := e'^{\mathsf T} G_1^{-1} e',
\]
with $e = (1, e')$ in the dual frame, $c$ and $B$ smooth up to the wall and $c = 0$ on $\Sig$; and the ambient form $h$ of the one-sided completion is nondegenerate of signature $(p{+}1, q{+}1)$ on all of $\Mp$, including $\Sig$. No order of vanishing of $S$ is used.
\item \emph{(Finite order.)} If moreover $S = \tau^m u$ with $m \geq 1$ finite and $u$ nowhere zero on $\Sig$, then for odd $m$ and good couplings the far-side degeneration of $h$ lies on a shadow wall $\Sig'$ across which $\det h$ has a simple zero, so $(T, h)$ is a tame corank-one degeneration along $\Sig'$ whatever $m$ is; for even $m$ the signature does not change across $\Sig$ and $h$ is nondegenerate on a whole neighbourhood of $\Sig$.
\item \emph{(Two sides.)} A wall across which the signature changes is two-sided, with or without (T3); at even order a one-sided wall carrying a corank-one degeneration exists.
\end{enumerate}
In particular the wild wall with $S = \tau^3$ violates (T3) and is completed by one rung, and its shadow wall is first order; what fails there is the simple pole of $G^{-1}$, which has order three.
synthesis.tameness-splits-regularity-and.technical:
Tameness is three clauses: (T1) the wall is a smooth closed hypersurface, (T2) the corank is exactly one with a smooth radical line bundle, (T3) the degeneration is first order. Write the Gram matrix along a transversal in a frame whose first vector spans the radical on the wall, and let $S$ be the Schur complement of the nondegenerate block, the dying eigenvalue up to a positive factor. By Jacobi's formula the differential of $\det G$ on the wall is the determinant of the nondegenerate block times the transversality datum at corank one, and zero at higher corank. So the three clauses together say exactly that the wall is the regular zero set of $\det G$, and (T3) says $S$ vanishes to first order. Whether tameness is generic, which turns on transverse corank-two points, is not addressed here (filed alongside, synthesis.transverse-corank-two-walls-are-wild).

The consumers use (T3) unevenly. The one-sided completion needs none of it: the exact identity $s = (1-c)^2/S + B$ replaces the expansion $s = 1/\lambda + O(1)$, and $s \to +\infty$ on the physical side whatever the order of vanishing. The wall iteration needs only finite order: the monotone zone exists because $s'$ is dominated by $-N S'/S^2$, and every shadow wall is then a simple zero of $\det h$, so the walls from the second on are tame automatically. Two-sidedness needs only that the signature changes. The canonical simple pole of $G^{-1}$, the identification of the conormal bundle with the square of the dying line, and the exceptional algebra of the normal-cone deformation do use first order in their stated proofs: at order $m$ the pole has order $m$. This consumer reading is an audit of the stated proofs, not a theorem.
synthesis.tameness-splits-regularity-and.lay: The series assumes that wherever its geometry degenerates, it does so in the tamest possible way: along a smooth wall, one direction at a time, with the dying length shrinking at a steady linear rate. This result takes that assumption apart. The first part says that it is the same as asking that a single number built from the geometry crosses zero cleanly. The linear-rate part is not needed for the main repair the series performs at a wall: a wall where the length dies like the cube of the distance is repaired by the same construction, and the next walls the repair creates are clean ones. What does use the linear rate, as the series' proofs are written, is the precise form of the blow-up of the inverse metric at the wall and the limiting algebra built from it.

\emph{Which consumers need which clause} (a reading of their stated proofs, not a theorem). The one-sided completion uses (T3) only through the expansion replaced in (2). The induction to shadow walls uses it only for the monotone zone, replaced in (3) by finite order. Two-sidedness follows from the signature change, (4). The absolute form of conservation of degeneracy uses only that the two sides carry different signatures. The degeneration sheaf uses (T1) and (T2). The canonical simple pole of $G^{-1}$, hence the identification $N^*\Sig \cong \shL^{\otimes 2}$ through the residue, and the exceptional algebra of the normal-cone deformation (whose rescaling $k \mapsto k/\sqrt t$ needs $\dot G(k,k) 
eq 0$) do use first order, as do the results that import that pole.

synthesis.transverse-corank-two-walls-ar.technical: Tameness asks three things of a degenerating cometric: a smooth wall, a corank-one radical line along it, and first-order vanishing. This result shows that they are not what a generic degeneration does once the dimension is at least three. At a transverse point where the cometric loses two directions at once, the determinant vanishes to second order, the degeneracy locus is a quadric cone rather than a smooth wall, and the radical has rank two; such points survive every small perturbation, so the tame cometrics are not dense. Three signatures meet at each such point, and if this world's signature $(1,3)$ is one of them, a two-time signature $(2,2)$ is another. On surfaces the phenomenon cannot occur and transverse degenerations are tame. Transport-absent.
synthesis.transverse-corank-two-walls-ar.lay: The series assumes that when the geometry of spacetime breaks down it does so along a smooth wall, losing one direction at a time and at a steady rate. This result shows that in three or more dimensions this is not what typically happens everywhere. At some places two directions can be lost at once, and no small change to the geometry removes such places: in four dimensions they form lines, the wall pinches into a cone there, and three kinds of geometry meet. Next to our kind of spacetime, one of the three always has two time directions.

proofs.main:
\emph{Frames.} A change of local frame acts on the matrix of $G$ by congruence, $G \mapsto P^{T} G P$ with $P$ invertible. Congruence is a diffeomorphism of the symmetric matrices that preserves corank and signature (\claimref{std-algebra.sylvester-inertia}), so it preserves each corank stratum, and transversality to a stratum is frame-independent; $\det G$ changes by the nonvanishing factor $\det(P)^2$, so its zero set and the order of vanishing are frame-independent.

\emph{Step 1: the Schur normal form.} Let $x$ have corank $r$ and choose a frame with $G_x = 0_r \oplus B_0$, $B_0$ nondegenerate of signature $(p_0, q_0)$. Near $x$ write $G = \begin{pmatrix} A & C \\ C^{T} & B \end{pmatrix}$ with $B$ invertible. Congruence by $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -B^{-1}C^{T} & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ carries $G$ to $S \oplus B$ with $S := A - C B^{-1} C^{T}$, a smooth $r \times r$ symmetric matrix function with $S(x) = 0$. Hence near $x$ the corank of $G$ is the corank of $S$, the signature of $G$ is $\mathrm{sig}(S) + (p_0, q_0)$, and $\det G = \det S \cdot \det B$. The map $(A, C, B) \mapsto S$ is a submersion near $G_x$ (its derivative in the $A$ direction is the identity), so near $G_x$ the corank-$r$ matrices are the preimage of $0$, a submanifold of codimension $\dim \mathrm{Sym}_r = r(r+1)/2$, and $G$ is transverse at $x$ exactly when $d(S \circ G)_x : T_xM \to \mathrm{Sym}_r$ is surjective.

\emph{Lemma A (corank one).} The regularity characterisation of tameness, (T1)-(T3) as the regular zero set of $\det G$, and the $r + 1$ signature count of Lemma B are also proved in the result filed alongside, synthesis.tameness-splits-regularity-and-order; they are repeated here in the form the stability argument uses. At corank one, $G_x\,\mathrm{adj}(G_x) = \det(G_x) = 0$, so every column of the adjugate lies in the kernel, spanned by $k$; the adjugate is symmetric and nonzero (a rank $n-1$ matrix has a nonzero $(n-1)$-minor), so $\mathrm{adj}(G_x) = c\,k k^{T}$ with $c \neq 0$. Jacobi's formula gives $d(\det G)_x = \mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{adj}(G_x)\, dG_x) = c\, k^{T} dG_x\, k$. Extending $k$ to a covector field and putting $g_k = G(k,k)$, $d(g_k)_x = k^{T} dG_x k + 2 k^{T} G_x\, dk = k^{T} dG_x k$, since $G_x k = 0$; this is $\delta(k \otimes k)$ at $x$ (Lemma \claimref{sheaf.invariant-form-t3}). So $d(\det G)_x = c\,\delta(k \otimes k)$, and (T3) of Hypotheses \claimref{sheaf.tameness} at $x$ is $d(\det G)_x \neq 0$. For $r = 1$ the stratum is locally $\{\det = 0\}$ with $d\det$ nonzero on it ($H \mapsto c\,k^{T} H k$), so transversality is again $d(\det \circ G)_x \neq 0$. Then $\Sig = (\det G)^{-1}(0)$ is a smooth hypersurface near $x$; corank at most one is an open condition, so $n - 1$ eigenvalues of $G$ stay away from zero near $x$ and the remaining one has the sign of $\det G$ divided by their product, which changes across $\Sig$ because the zero of $\det G$ is simple. The two sides therefore carry $(p_0 + 1, q_0)$ and $(p_0, q_0 + 1)$. The check \texttt{check\_corank\_one\_differential\_is\_delta} verifies $\mathrm{adj}(G_0) = c\,kk^{T}$, $c \neq 0$, and that the $t$-coefficient of $\det(G_0 + tH)$ is $c\,H(k,k)$, for six corank-one cometrics and four directions each, including directions with $H(k,k) = 0$; \texttt{check\_tame\_wall\_is\_two\_signature} verifies the signature jump.

\emph{Lemma B (signatures), which is clause (2).} If $G$ is transverse at $x$ then $S \circ G$ is a submersion at $x$, so by the submersion theorem it maps every neighbourhood of $x$ onto a neighbourhood of $0$ in $\mathrm{Sym}_r$. That neighbourhood contains $\varepsilon\,\mathrm{diag}(1, \dots, 1, -1, \dots, -1)$ with $j$ entries $-1$, for each $j = 0, \dots, r$ and small $\varepsilon > 0$; there $G$ has signature $(p_0 + r - j, q_0 + j)$. For $r = 2$ these are $(p_0 + 2, q_0)$, $(p_0 + 1, q_0 + 1)$, $(p_0, q_0 + 2)$. If $(1,3)$ is among them then $(p_0, q_0)$ is $(0,2)$ or $(1,1)$ (the first entry cannot be $p_0 + 2 = 1$ with $p_0 + q_0 = 2$ unless $p_0 = -1$), and in both cases $(2,2)$ is in the list. The check \texttt{check\_transverse\_corank\_two\_three\_signatures} computes the three signatures exactly for three blocks $B$ at three scales, and the count $r + 1$ for $r = 1, 2, 3$.

\emph{Clause (1), the cone.} Transversality at corank two needs a surjection $T_xM \to \mathrm{Sym}_2 \cong \R^3$, so $n \geq 3$. By the submersion theorem there are coordinates $(y_1, y_2, y_3, z)$, $z \in \R^{n-3}$, centred at $x$ with $S \circ G = \begin{pmatrix} y_1 & y_2 \\ y_2 & y_3\end{pmatrix}$. Then $\det G = (y_1 y_3 - y_2^2)\det B$ with $\det B \neq 0$, which vanishes to second order at $x$, and $\Sig$ is the cone $y_1 y_3 = y_2^2$ (a quadric of signature $(1,2)$: $y_1 y_3 - y_2^2 = \tfrac14(y_1 + y_3)^2 - \tfrac14(y_1 - y_3)^2 - y_2^2$) times $\R^{n-3}$. It contains the lines through $x$ in the directions $(1,1,1,0)$, $(1,-1,1,0)$, $(4,2,1,0)$ and every $z$ direction, which together span $T_xM$; a smooth hypersurface through $x$ contains only curves tangent to its $(n-1)$-dimensional tangent space there, so $\Sig$ is not a smooth hypersurface at $x$ and (T1) fails. The radical of $G_x$ has rank two, so (T2) fails. The check \texttt{check\_cone\_is\_not\_a\_hypersurface} verifies, in the model with $n = 4$, that the linear coefficient of $\det G(tv)$ vanishes in six directions while a quadratic one does not, that the four lines lie in $\Sig$ and span $\R^4$, and that the corank-two locus is the $z$-line.

\emph{Clause (1), stability.} Let $G'$ be a cometric with $\|G' - G\|_{C^1} < \eta$ on a closed coordinate ball $\bar U$ about $x$. For small $\eta$ the block $B'$ stays invertible on $\bar U$ and the Schur complement $S'$ of $G'$ (a smooth function of the matrix entries) satisfies $\|S' - S\|_{C^1(\bar U)} \leq K\eta$ for a constant $K$ fixed by $G$ on $\bar U$. Fix $z_0$ near $0$ and work on the ball $|y| \leq \rho$ inside $\bar U$, where $S(y, z_0) = y$ in the identification $\mathrm{Sym}_2 \cong \R^3$ above. The map $T(y) = y - S'(y, z_0) = (S - S')(y, z_0)$ has Lipschitz constant at most $K\eta$ and moves no point by more than $K\eta$; for $K\eta \leq \min(\tfrac12, \tfrac{\rho}{2})$ it maps the ball into itself and is a contraction, so it has a unique fixed point $y^{*}$, $|y^{*}| \leq 2K\eta$, where $S' = 0$, that is where $G'$ has corank two. There $d_y S' = 1 - d_yT$ is within $\tfrac12$ of the identity, hence invertible, so $G'$ is transverse at $(y^{*}, z_0)$. The check \texttt{check\_corank\_two\_point\_survives\_perturbation} exhibits the persisting corank-two point exactly, by solving $S' = 0$, for two constant perturbations at $\varepsilon = 10^{-1}, 10^{-2}, 10^{-3}$ (with $|y^{*}| \leq 10\varepsilon$) and for a position-dependent perturbation of the $A$ block at three values of $z$.

\emph{Clause (1), conclusion, and clause (3).} The corank-two points of a cometric transverse to the corank-two stratum are the preimage of that stratum, a submanifold of codimension three. Let $G$ be transverse at every point of $\Sig$. At a point of corank $r \geq 2$ Lemma B puts at least three signatures in every neighbourhood and the cone argument shows (T1) and (T2) fail there (for $r > 2$ the radical has rank $r$ and (T2) fails directly). At a point of corank at most one some neighbourhood meets at most two signatures by Lemma A, and if every point of $\Sig$ has corank one then Lemma A gives (T1) and (T3) everywhere on $\Sig$ ($\Sig$ is the zero set of $\det G$, hence closed, and a regular zero set, hence a smooth hypersurface), while the radical lines are the kernel of a smooth family of constant rank $n - 1$ on $\Sig$ (locally the span of a nonzero column of the adjugate), a smooth line subbundle, which is (T2). So the points where tameness fails are exactly the points near which three or more signatures meet. For $n = 2$ there is no surjection $T_xM \to \mathrm{Sym}_2$, so a transverse cometric on a surface has no corank-two point and is tame. For $n \geq 3$ the model of the cone argument is transverse at the origin and by the stability argument every cometric $C^1$-close to it on $\bar U$ has a corank-two point, so it is not tame: the non-tame cometrics contain a nonempty open set, and tameness is not generic.

\emph{Remark (argued, not part of the claim).} Every transverse corank-two point adjacent to this world's signature $(1,3)$ opens a $(2,2)$ region, a residue-$0$ signature with two times. The series excludes two-time signatures for the $r = 0$ tower by an imported instability of two-time dynamics. If that exclusion is extended to regions of one spacetime, transverse corank-two points next to $(1,3)$ are ruled out, and for degenerations transverse along $\Sig$ the clauses above then give tameness near every point of $\Sig$ adjacent to $(1,3)$. Whether the exclusion may be read that way is a decision about the premise, not a theorem here.

synthesis.twisted-wall-induction-conserv.technical: The wall-class conjecture asks for a torsion-sensitive invariant of tame walls that is conserved under the wall induction. The earlier one-rung result identified the torsion part as the first Stiefel-Whitney class of the dying line, which obstructs the untwisted one-rung completion and forces a twisted rung to use a line bundle extending the dying line. This result runs the induction with that twisted rung. Locally the twisted ambient form is the untwisted one, and the sign ambiguity of the twisting line acts by a reflection of the adjoined plane that preserves the form, so the shadow wall exists and is tame exactly as before. Its radical line is computed explicitly: its cotangent component is the metric dual of the twisted transversal, which carries the twist, so the new dying line is a copy of the twisting line. Hence the class is carried unchanged to every shadow wall, the same line bundle twists every later rung, and the pair made of the signature mismatch and this class is constant along the wall sequence. An explicit torus wall whose dying direction turns by half a revolution around one circle realises a nonzero class.
synthesis.twisted-wall-induction-conserv.lay: Where the geometry changes signature, the direction that dies can twist like a Moebius band as one goes around the wall. An earlier result showed that this twist blocks the most economical repair unless the extra directions added by the repair are twisted in the same way. This result follows the repair forward. Each repair creates a new wall a little further into the unphysical region, and the direction that dies there turns out to twist in exactly the same way as before. So the twist is never removed; it is handed on from wall to wall, as the series' principle that obstructions are moved rather than destroyed expects. A concrete example on a doughnut-shaped wall shows the twist really occurs.

h =  egin{pmatrix} G &  eta

u e^{\mathsf T} & 0 & 1 \  eta\mu e^{\mathsf T} & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The other unit frame is $-\lambda_0$, which sends $e \mapsto -e$, $n_o \mapsto -n_o$, $n_\infty \mapsto -n_\infty$, and $D h(e) D = h(-e)$ for $D = 1 \oplus (-1) \oplus (-1)$ (checked): the form is frame-independent, so $h$ is a well-defined symmetric form on $T_\Lambda$. Thus $\xi \mapsto$ (that vector) is a bundle isomorphism $\Lambda^*|_{\Sig'} 	o \shL'$. Real line bundles are self-dual (a fibre metric), so $\shL' \cong \Lambda|_{\Sig'}$. synthesis.wall-class-one-rung-obstructio.formal:
Let $(M, G)$ be a tame corank-one degeneration (Hypotheses \claimref{sheaf.tameness}) with $M$ connected and without boundary, $\Sig$ compact and separating $M$ into a physical side $\Mp$ and a far side, both nonempty, with signatures $(p,q)$ and $(p{-}1,q{+}1)$; let $\shL \subset T^*M|_\Sig$ be the radical line bundle and fix a collar $C \cong \Sig \times [-1,1]$, $\Sig = \Sig \times \{0\}$, the physical side at positive parameter. Write $H$ for the hyperbolic form on the trivial plane $\underline{\R}^2$ and call $T := T^*M \oplus \underline{\R}^2$ the one-rung bundle.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{(Strict reading.)} No smooth symmetric form on any bundle $E \supset T^*M$ that equals $G \perp K$ outside $C$ with one signature of $K$ on both exterior regions is nondegenerate everywhere (Theorem \claimref{sheaf.conservation-degeneracy-absolute-form}). The obstruction is the clock mismatch $2 \in \mathbb{Z}_8$, which is nonzero for every tame wall with two nonempty sides; so on every tame wall satisfying these hypotheses the condition in clause (a) of Conjecture \claimref{sheaf.wall-class} fails, whatever the torsion of $(\shL, N^*\Sig)$.
\item \emph{(Full relaxation.)} If the exterior model may change signature across the wall, nothing obstructs: for any bundle metric $A$ on $T^*M$ and any bump $\beta$ equal to $1$ near $\Sig$ and $0$ outside $C$, the form
\[
h_D(\alpha \oplus \alpha', \gamma \oplus \gamma') \;=\; G(\alpha,\gamma) - G(\alpha',\gamma') + \beta\bigl(A(\alpha,\gamma') + A(\alpha',\gamma)\bigr)
\]
on $T^*M \oplus T^*M$ is nondegenerate of signature $(n,n)$ at every point of $M$, and equals $G \perp (-G)$ outside $C$.
\item \emph{(One rung, two sides.)} There is a smooth symmetric form $h$ on $T$, nondegenerate at every point of $M$, equal to $G \perp H$ outside $C$ on the physical side and to $G \perp K_-$ outside $C$ on the far side with $K_-$ positive definite, if and only if $w_1(\shL) = 0$. The same holds with the roles exchanged ($H$ on the far side, a negative definite plane on the physical side), with $h|_{T^*M} = G$ in the construction.
\item \emph{(One rung, one side.)} There is a smooth symmetric form $h$ on $T$ over $\Mp$, nondegenerate at every point of $\Mp$ including $\Sig$, with $h|_{T^*M} = G$ along $\Sig$ and $h = G \perp H$ outside $C$, if and only if $w_1(\shL) = 0$. The standing hypothesis of Theorem \claimref{sheaf.one-sided-completion} is therefore necessary for every one-sided one-rung completion, not only for the coupling construction.
\item \emph{(Twisted rung.)} If the adjoined plane is $\Lambda \oplus \Lambda^*$ with its hyperbolic pairing, for a line bundle $\Lambda$ over $\Mp$, a form as in (4) with $\Lambda \oplus \Lambda^*$ in place of $\underline{\R}^2$ exists only if $\Lambda|_\Sig \cong \shL$. In particular a twisted one-sided completion requires $w_1(\shL)$ to lie in the image of the restriction $H^1(\Mp; \mathbb{Z}_2) \to H^1(\Sig; \mathbb{Z}_2)$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently the pair $W(\Sig) := (w(\Sig), w_1(\shL))$ has a precise meaning: its coarse part obstructs the strict two-sided completion and is never zero on a two-sided wall; its torsion part obstructs exactly the one-rung completions, one-sided or two-sided; and no torsion-sensitive class can be characterised by clause (a) of Conjecture \claimref{sheaf.wall-class} in either reading of ``standard''.
synthesis.wall-class-one-rung-obstructio.technical:
The wall-class conjecture asks for a torsion-sensitive invariant of a tame wall, refining the signature mismatch, whose vanishing is equivalent to the existence of a completion nondegenerate on both sides. This result shows that the equivalence as posed cannot involve torsion, and locates where torsion does act. In the strict reading (one exterior model on both sides) the signature count always obstructs; in the fully relaxed reading (the added form may change signature across the wall) a doubling of the cotangent bundle removes every obstruction. Between the two, with exactly one adjoined hyperbolic plane, the obstruction is exactly the first Stiefel-Whitney class of the dying line: a two-sided completion that is standard on the physical side and positive definite on the far side exists if and only if $w_1(\shL) = 0$, and so does any one-sided one-rung completion that restricts to $G$ along the wall. With a twisted plane $\Lambda \oplus \Lambda^*$ the dying line must extend over the physical side.

The necessity proofs compare negative eigenbundles across the collar: on the physical exterior the negative bundle is that of the induced form on $T^*M/\shL$ plus the trivial negative line of $H$; on the far side, or at the wall itself, it is the same bundle plus a line isomorphic to $\shL$; comparing determinant lines gives $\shL$ trivial. The sufficiency in (3) is an explicit construction from the collar data, with a coupling small enough in the sense of the good-coupling bound.
synthesis.wall-class-one-rung-obstructio.lay: At a tame wall where the geometry changes signature, earlier results showed that a repair which looks the same on both sides must fail somewhere. This result asks what happens if the repair may look different on the two sides. With unlimited room, everything can be repaired, so that version of the question detects nothing. With the room the series actually uses, one extra pair of directions, and keeping the original geometry unchanged at the wall itself, a repair exists exactly when the direction that dies at the wall does not twist like a Moebius band as one goes around the wall. That twist is the subtle topological invariant the conjecture was looking for; it decides the economical repair, not the strict one.

proofs.main:
\emph{Two elementary tools.} (a) \emph{Negative bundles.} For a nondegenerate symmetric form on a vector bundle over a compact base, a maximal negative definite subbundle exists (the negative eigenspaces with respect to an auxiliary bundle metric), and any two are isomorphic: the space of maximal negative subspaces of a fixed fibre is contractible, and more concretely, if $N_1, N_2$ are maximal negative subspaces, the projection onto $N_1$ along its $h$-orthogonal complement $N_1^{\perp_h}$ (which is positive definite) restricts to an isomorphism $N_2 \to N_1$: its kernel on $N_2$ is $N_2 \cap N_1^{\perp_h}$, negative and positive definite at once, hence zero, and the dimensions agree. Write $N(h)$ for this bundle. (b) \emph{Continuity along a collar.} If $V_t$, $t \in [0,1]$, is a continuous family of subbundles of a fixed bundle over a compact base, then $V_0 \cong V_1$: with orthogonal projections $\pi_t$ for an auxiliary metric, $\pi_t|_{V_s} : V_s \to V_t$ is an isomorphism when $\|\pi_t - \pi_s\| < 1$, uniform continuity on $[0,1]$ gives finitely many steps, and composing them gives the isomorphism. Over the collar, transport along the lines $\{x\} \times [-1,1]$ for any connection identifies $T|_C$ with the pullback of $T|_\Sig$, so a subbundle of $T|_C$ is a continuous family of subbundles of $T|_\Sig$ and (b) applies to it. Finally, isomorphic bundles have isomorphic determinant lines, $\det(N \oplus \ell) \cong \det N \otimes \ell$ for a line bundle $\ell$, $\ell \otimes \ell$ is trivial for every real line bundle and a line bundle is trivial iff its $w_1$ vanishes (Fact \claimref{sheaf.imported-real-line-bundles}).

\emph{The negative bundle of $G$ near the wall.} Throughout, $(M,G)$ satisfies (T1) to (T3) (\claimref{sheaf.tameness}). Let $\tilde\shL$ be a line subbundle of $T^*M|_C$ extending $\shL$ and $Q$ a complement. Along $\Sig$, $Q \cong T^*M/\shL$ and $G|_Q$ is the induced form $\overline G$, nondegenerate of signature $(p{-}1,q)$ by Theorem \claimref{sheaf.degeneration-sheaf}(2); by compactness $G|_Q$ is nondegenerate on a thinner collar $C_0 = \Sig \times [-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]$. Then $T^*M = Q \oplus Q^{\perp_G}$ on $C_0$, the line $Q^{\perp_G}$ is isomorphic to $T^*M/Q \cong \tilde\shL$ and equals $\shL$ on $\Sig$, and $G$ restricted to it is the Schur complement $\hat\lambda$, which has the sign of the dying eigenvalue: positive on the physical side and negative on the far side (the signatures are $(p,q)$ and $(p{-}1,q{+}1)$ and $G|_Q$ has constant signature). Hence, with $N_Q := N(G|_Q)$, a rank-$q$ bundle on $C_0$ restricting to $N(\overline G)$ on $\Sig$,
\[
N(G) \cong N_Q \ \text{on the physical half of } C_0 \setminus \Sig, \qquad N(G) \cong N_Q \oplus \tilde\shL \ \text{on the far half}.
\]
Since $G$ is nondegenerate on each half of $C \setminus \Sig$, tool (b) carries these isomorphisms from $\Sig \times \{\pm\varepsilon\}$ to $\Sig \times \{\pm 1\}$. The check verifies the underlying inertia additivity $\operatorname{In}(G) = \operatorname{In}(G|_Q) + \operatorname{sign}\hat\lambda$ on fixed rational instances.

\emph{(1)} is Theorem \claimref{sheaf.conservation-degeneracy-absolute-form}: the totals $(p,q) + \operatorname{sig}K$ and $(p{-}1,q{+}1) + \operatorname{sig}K$ differ, and in clock terms the two sides sit at $d$ and $d - 2$, with $2 \neq 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_8$. Both sides being nonempty is the only hypothesis, so the existence question of clause (a) is decided by the coarse data alone.

\emph{(2)} At a point, choose an $A$-orthonormal frame, so that $G$ has a symmetric Gram matrix $S$ and $h_D$ has Gram $D = \begin{psmallmatrix} S & \beta 1 \\ \beta 1 & -S \end{psmallmatrix}$. Then $D^2 = (S^2 + \beta^2) \oplus (S^2 + \beta^2)$. Where $\beta \neq 0$ this is positive definite, so $D$ is invertible; where $\beta = 0$ the point lies off $\Sig$, $S$ is invertible and $D = S \oplus (-S)$ is invertible. The map $J(\alpha,\alpha') = (\alpha', -\alpha)$ satisfies $J^{\mathsf T} D J = -D$ in such a frame, so the spectrum of $D$ is symmetric and the signature is $(n,n)$. Outside $C$, $h_D = G \perp (-G)$, whose second summand has signature $(q,p)$ on the physical side and $(q{+}1,p{-}1)$ on the far side.

\emph{(3), necessity.} Let $h$ be as stated and $V := N(h)$, a bundle over $M$ of rank $q + 1$ (on the physical exterior $h = G \perp H$ has signature $(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, and $M$ is connected). On $\Sig \times \{1\}$, $V \cong N(G) \oplus N(H) \cong N_Q|_{\Sig \times \{1\}} \oplus \underline{\R}$, and on $\Sig \times \{-1\}$, $V \cong N(G) \oplus N(K_-) = N(G) \cong N_Q|_{\Sig \times \{-1\}} \oplus \tilde\shL|_{\Sig \times \{-1\}}$. By tool (b) applied to $V$, $N_Q$ and $\tilde\shL$ over $C$, all identified with bundles over $\Sig$,
\[
N(\overline G) \oplus \underline{\R} \;\cong\; N(\overline G) \oplus \shL .
\]
Taking determinant lines, $\det N(\overline G) \cong \det N(\overline G) \otimes \shL$, and tensoring with $\det N(\overline G)$ (whose square is trivial) gives $\shL \cong \underline{\R}$, so $w_1(\shL) = 0$. The necessity half of the exchanged statement is the same computation with the two exteriors interchanged.

\emph{(3), sufficiency.} Let $w_1(\shL) = 0$ and take collar data $(k, u, \beta, \mu)$ (Definition \claimref{obj.sheaf.collar-data-coupling}). In the plane use the basis $a = \nO + \nInf$, $b = \nO - \nInf$, in which $H = \operatorname{diag}(-2, 2)$. For a smooth function $\varsigma$ with values in $[-1,1]$ set $K_\varsigma := \operatorname{diag}(-2\varsigma, 2)$ and
\[
h \;:=\; G \perp K_\varsigma + \kappa_a, \qquad \kappa_a(\alpha, a) = \mu\beta\,\alpha(u), \quad \kappa_a(\alpha, b) = 0 ,
\]
so $h = G \perp H$ where $\beta = 0$, $\varsigma = 1$ and $h = G \perp \operatorname{diag}(2,2)$ where $\beta = 0$, $\varsigma = -1$. Off $\Sig$ the Schur complement of the $G$-block, as in Lemma \claimref{sheaf.determinant-identity-blow-up-expansion}(1), gives
\[
\det h \;=\; \det G \cdot 2\,\bigl(-2\varsigma - \mu^2\beta^2 s\bigr), \qquad s = G^{-1}(e,e) = \frac1\lambda + O(1)
\]
(Lemma \claimref{sheaf.determinant-identity-blow-up-expansion}(2)). Let $S$ bound $|s|$ on the support of $\beta$ outside a fixed thin neighbourhood $Z$ of $\Sig$ inside $\{\beta = 1\}$ on which $s$ has the sign of the side (finite by compactness, as in Lemma \claimref{sheaf.tame-wall-induction}; $s$ may change sign outside $Z$), and choose $\mu$ with $\mu^2 S < 2$. Put $Z' := \Sig \cup (\{|s| > 2/\mu^2\} \cap Z)$, a neighbourhood of $\Sig$ inside $Z \subset \{\beta = 1\}$ (since $|s| \to \infty$ at the wall, uniformly by compactness); and take $\varsigma = 1$ on the physical side outside $Z'$, $\varsigma = -1$ on the far side outside $Z'$. Then $-2\varsigma - \mu^2\beta^2 s \neq 0$ off $\Sig$: where $\beta = 0$ it is $\mp 2$; on the support of $\beta$ outside $Z$ it is at most $-2 + \mu^2 S < 0$ (physical) or at least $2 - \mu^2 S > 0$ (far); on $Z \setminus Z'$, $\beta = 1$ and $s$ has the side's sign, giving $-2 - \mu^2 s < 0$ or $2 + \mu^2|s| > 0$; on $Z' \setminus \Sig$, $|\varsigma| \le 1$ and $\mu^2|s| > 2$ give $-2\varsigma - \mu^2 s \le 2 - \mu^2 s < 0$ (physical) and $\ge -2 + \mu^2|s| > 0$ (far). On $\Sig$, as in Lemma \claimref{sheaf.wall-gram}, $T = V_1 \oplus \operatorname{span}(k, a, b)$ orthogonally, $h|_{V_1} = \overline G$ is nondegenerate, and the block of $(k, a, b)$ has Gram $\begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & \mu & 0 \\ \mu & -2\varsigma & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{psmallmatrix}$ with determinant $-2\mu^2 \neq 0$ for every value of $\varsigma$. So $h$ is nondegenerate everywhere, of signature $(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, standard on the physical exterior and positive definite in the plane on the far exterior. The check runs this construction exactly along a model transversal on which $s$ changes sign inside the collar, including the interpolation zone and the wall, and confirms that it degenerates when $\mu^2 S \ge 2$.

\emph{(3), sufficiency of the exchanged statement.} $-G$ is a tame corank-one degeneration with the same radical line $\shL$, whose physical side (where its dying eigenvalue is positive) is the far side of $G$, of signature $(q, p)$ there. The construction applied to $-G$ gives $h'$ on $T$, nondegenerate, with $h'|_{T^*M} = -G$, equal to $(-G) \perp H$ outside $C$ on the far side of $G$ and to $(-G) \perp K'$ with $K'$ positive definite on the physical side. Then $h := -h'$ restricts to $G$ on $T^*M$, equals $G \perp (-H)$ on the far exterior and $G \perp (-K')$, with $-K'$ negative definite, on the physical exterior; and $-H \cong H$ by $\nInf \mapsto -\nInf$.

\emph{(4).} Sufficiency is Theorem \claimref{sheaf.one-sided-completion}. Necessity: let $h$ be as stated and $V = N(h)$ over $\Mp$, of rank $q + 1$. On $\Sig \times \{1\}$, $V \cong N_Q \oplus \underline{\R}$ as in (3). At $\Sig$, $h|_{T^*M} = G$ makes $\shL$ isotropic and $h$-orthogonal to $T^*M$; with $V_1$ a complement of $\shL$ in $T^*M|_\Sig$, $h|_{V_1} = \overline G$ is nondegenerate and $T|_\Sig = V_1 \oplus W$, $W := V_1^{\perp_h}$ of rank three, nondegenerate, containing $\shL$, of signature $(p{+}1,q{+}1) - (p{-}1,q) = (2,1)$. In $W$, $\shL^{\perp}$ has rank two and radical $\shL$, so $\ell := \shL^\perp/\shL$ is a nondegenerate line and $W = \ell' \perp P$ with $\ell' \cong \ell$ and $P := \ell'^{\perp}$ a plane of signature $(1,1)$ containing the isotropic line $\shL$; the signature count forces $\ell$ positive. The negative line $N(W) = N(P)$ meets $\shL$ trivially, so it maps isomorphically onto $P/\shL$, which $h$ pairs nondegenerately with $\shL$ ($\shL^{\perp_P} = \shL$): $N(W) \cong P/\shL \cong \shL^* \cong \shL$, the partner line of the residue theorem (\claimref{sheaf.metrics-residue-square-root-twist}) in this setting. Hence $V|_\Sig \cong N(\overline G) \oplus \shL$. Tool (b) on the physical half of $C$ gives $N(\overline G) \oplus \shL \cong N(\overline G) \oplus \underline{\R}$, and the determinant argument of (3) gives $w_1(\shL) = 0$. The check verifies on the wall Gram of Lemma \claimref{sheaf.wall-gram} that the isotropic line's orthogonal is positive, so the negative line pairs with $\shL$.

\emph{(5).} The same argument with $\Lambda \oplus \Lambda^*$ in place of $\underline{\R}^2$: the negative line of the hyperbolic plane $\Lambda \oplus \Lambda^*$ meets the isotropic line $\Lambda$ trivially and so is isomorphic to $(\Lambda \oplus \Lambda^*)/\Lambda = \Lambda^* \cong \Lambda$; hence $V|_{\Sig \times \{1\}} \cong N_Q \oplus \Lambda$, and the comparison at $\Sig$ gives $\det N(\overline G) \otimes \shL \cong \det N(\overline G) \otimes \Lambda|_\Sig$, that is $\shL \cong \Lambda|_\Sig$. A line bundle on $\Sig$ extends over $\Mp$ exactly when its class lies in the image of the restriction on $H^1(\,\cdot\,; \mathbb{Z}_2)$, line bundles being classified by $w_1$ (Fact \claimref{sheaf.imported-real-line-bundles}).

\emph{The consequence.} By (1), clause (a)'s condition fails on every wall satisfying the hypotheses (both sides nonempty), whatever the torsion; by (2), dropping the single exterior model leaves nothing to obstruct; by (3) and (4), at one rung the obstruction is exactly $w_1(\shL)$. Along the wall sequence of the untwisted completion the pair $W(\Sig)$ is carried unchanged: the rung shifts $(p,q)$ by $(1,1)$ and preserves both clock positions, and the shadow wall's radical line has the global spanning section of the proof of the infinite wall sequence, so its $w_1$ is $0$ (Theorem \claimref{sheaf.infinite-wall-sequence}), as is that of $\shL$ under the standing hypothesis; conservation for twisted sequences is open.
